query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K), the maintenance of a stable single-phase solid solution in equiatomic multimetal nanoparticles is governed by the interplay between high configurational entropy and the suppression of atomic diffusion. When the constituent metals have similar diffusion kinetics and moderate atomic size differences (which promote strong lattice distortion and high kinetic barriers), the high entropy effectively stabilizes the homogeneous structure. However, if one or more metals diffuses significantly faster due to larger atomic size mismatches or less favorable mixing enthalpies, local phase segregation or intermetallic formation will occur.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equiatomic ratios that form a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Subject the nanoparticles to thermal cycling or steady-state heating up to 1923 K in atmospheres representative of catalytic or thermoelectric operating conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in controlled (inert or mildly reactive) atmospheres with carefully regulated temperature ramp rates and dwell times, minimizing any extraneous chemical driving forces such as aggressive oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale mixing maintained by high configurational entropy together with kinetic barriers induced by lattice distortion and similar diffusion rates among constituent metals.
generation.mechanism: High configururational entropy lowers the free energy of the homogeneous solid solution, while lattice distortions and similar atomic diffusion kinetics create energy barriers that slow atomic migration at elevated temperatures. If these barriers are sufficient, atomic rearrangements are suppressed, preserving phase homogeneity. On the other hand, significant differences in diffusion kinetics can locally overcome the entropy stabilization, leading to phase segregation or the formation of secondary phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles where the constituent metals exhibit similar diffusion behavior and moderate atomic size differences will retain a uniform single-phase structure and stable catalytic/thermoelectric performance. In contrast, formulations with pronounced differences in diffusion rates (or larger size mismatches) will develop detectable phase segregation and associated degradation in performance relative to the initial state.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized, homogeneous single-phase solid solution structure of the nanoparticles before thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: The prediction applies under thermal conditions typical of catalytic and thermoelectric applications and in atmospheres that do not introduce additional reactive species capable of independently driving phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold at which diffusion differences become critical and the quantitative extent of performance degradation remain uncertain and may vary with the specific elemental combinations and processing nuances.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one set formulated with constituent metals selected to have similar diffusion kinetics and moderate atomic size differences, and a second set intentionally incorporating one or more metals with higher diffusion coefficients and larger atomic size mismatches. Subject both sets to identical thermal protocols (ramping and steady-state heating up to 1923 K) under controlled catalytic/thermoelectric-simulating atmospheres. Monitor the structural and compositional evolution in situ using techniques such as high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with elemental mapping, and measure corresponding catalytic/thermoelectric performance.
measurements: In situ XRD for detection of new phase formation or peak shifts.
TEM with elemental mapping (EDS or APT) to observe atomic-scale chemical segregation.
Performance metrics (e.g., catalytic activity or thermoelectric efficiency) correlated with observed structural changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles designed with similar diffusion kinetics and moderate atomic size differences display significant phase segregation or degradation in functional performance, or if those designed with pronounced diffusion differences maintain a stable single-phase structure with unimpaired performance throughout the temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Unlike traditional alloys, which are normally based on one or two principal elements, HEAs defined by Yeh et al. can have five or more principal elements in equal or near-equal molar ratios. In recent studies, quaternary and ternary alloys in an equal molar ratio are also considered as HEAs,. The presence of multiple principal elements in HEAs is not merely a difference in composition, but has fundamental physical effects on the configurational entropy, free energy, phase selection, and stability. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are solid solutions consisting of five or more metallic elements in approximately equimolar ratios with elemental compositions typically between 5–35 atomic percent (at.%). They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature. drafts.hypothesis: In equiatomic multi‐metal nanoparticles that initially form a single-phase solid solution, the balance between high configurational entropy and the metals’ differing mixing enthalpies and atomic sizes governs structural and chemical stability at high temperatures: under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K), accelerated surface and bulk diffusion will selectively allow atoms with larger size mismatches or less favorable mixing enthalpies to segregate, thereby destabilizing the homogeneous structure.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution (e.g., a single FCC phase) with uniform elemental distribution.
drafts.intervention: Expose the nanoparticles to controlled temperature ramps reaching up to 1923 K under catalytic or thermoelectric operating conditions, while also comparing formulations with small variations in atomic size mismatches.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted in controlled atmospheres (inert or reactive as appropriate) with well-defined heating profiles ensuring sufficient residence time at target temperatures; no extraneous dopants or contaminants that could independently encourage phase separation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local atomic diffusion pathways—particularly those at particle surfaces—and the extent of atomic size mismatch and related mixing enthalpies that mediate diffusion kinetics and phase stability.
drafts.mechanism: At elevated operating temperatures, diffusion processes (especially surface diffusion) are activated. If a nanoparticle’s constituent metals possess significant differences in atomic sizes and mixing enthalpies, these differences lower local diffusion barriers and facilitate atomic rearrangements. This results in local phase separation or formation of intermetallic clusters that disrupt the initial solid solution. Conversely, when the differences are minimal, the high configurational entropy dominates, and the homogeneous phase is retained.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with more compatible atomic sizes and modest mixing enthalpy differences will maintain a single-phase solid solution structure (as evidenced by unchanged XRD patterns and uniform elemental distributions), while those with pronounced differences will show new diffraction peaks, elemental segregation, or the emergence of intermetallic phases correlated with variations in catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
drafts.baseline: The as-synthesized nanoparticles showing uniform single-phase solid solution characteristics (e.g., single-phase XRD, homogeneous elemental mapping via EDX or APT) and expected catalytic/thermoelectric activity.
drafts.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold under controlled synthesis conditions and typical industrial operating atmospheres; however, it may not apply if additional environmental factors (such as oxidation or exposure to reactive species) independently drive phase changes or if intentional dopants are introduced that alter diffusion kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare batches of equiatomic multi-metal nanoparticles with known degrees of atomic size/enthalpy mismatch. Subject each batch to a stepwise temperature increase (e.g., 473, 773, 1073, 1433, and 1923 K) under identical controlled atmospheres. Utilize X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), and atom probe tomography (APT) to track structural and compositional changes. Simultaneously, measure catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
measurements: XRD for phase changes (emergence of additional peaks or shifts in peak positions)
TEM/EDX mapping for localized phase segregation or elemental clustering
Atom probe tomography for atomic scale distribution
Catalytic/thermoelectric performance metrics correlating with structural changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles characterized by significant atomic size and mixing enthalpy differences retain a homogeneous solid solution across the full operating temperature range, or if nanoparticles with minimal differences unexpectedly exhibit phase segregation (and related performance changes), then the hypothesis that these inherent material contrasts mediate stability through diffusion-activated segregation is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles, structural and chemical stability across catalytic and thermoelectric temperatures (473–1923 K) is governed by the interplay between the stabilization imparted by high configurational entropy and the differential atomic diffusion kinetics of the constituent metals. When the atomic diffusion rates of the metals are relatively similar (or sufficiently slow relative to the applied thermal energy), the high entropy of mixing can maintain a solid solution structure; however, if one or more metals diffuses markedly faster than the others, the resulting mismatch can overcome entropy stabilization, leading to phase segregation or intermetallic formation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
drafts.intervention: Exposure to thermal conditions mimicking catalytic and thermoelectric operating environments (heating up to 1923 K) under a controlled gas atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Experiments should be conducted in atmospheres relevant to catalytic or thermoelectric applications (e.g., inert or controlled reactive environments) with careful control over temperature ramp rates and dwell times to isolate the effect of differential diffusion kinetics.
drafts.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale mixing and diffusion barriers that either promote uniformity (when diffusion differences are low) or allow phase segregation (when certain metals diffuse faster than others).
drafts.mechanism: High configurational entropy distributes thermal energy uniformly, suppressing phase separation as long as constituent atoms exhibit similar or slow diffusion rates. However, if specific metals have significantly higher diffusion coefficients at elevated temperatures, localized enrichment or depletion can occur, breaking the entropy stabilization and leading to the formation of secondary phases or intermetallic compounds.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under controlled thermal conditions, nanoparticles in which the individual metals have similar diffusion kinetics will retain their single-phase solid solution structure and exhibit consistent catalytic/thermoelectric performance relative to the initial state. In contrast, if there are significant differences in diffusion rates among the metals, evidence of phase segregation—detected by structural and compositional mapping—will correlate with reduced performance stability.
drafts.baseline: The initial homogeneous solid solution structure of the high-entropy nanoparticles before thermal treatment.
drafts.boundary: This prediction holds under operating conditions where the external environment does not introduce additional driving forces (such as aggressive oxidation) that independently cause phase change. The hypothesis is limited to diffusion-mediated effects in the temperature range of 473–1923 K.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles: one with metals chosen to have minimal differences in atomic diffusion coefficients, and another with a deliberate inclusion of a metal known to have a significantly higher diffusion coefficient. Subject both sets to identical heating protocols under catalytic/thermoelectric-relevant atmospheres (e.g., in-situ heating in a transmission electron microscope equipped with X-ray diffraction capabilities). Monitor structural changes in real time.
measurements: In-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to track phase changes over the temperature range.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with elemental mapping to identify phase segregation or secondary phase formation.
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance metrics correlated with structural observations.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with minimal expected diffusion disparities exhibit significant phase segregation or formation of secondary phases (or show a marked decline in performance), or if nanoparticles with intentionally high diffusion disparities remain as stable single-phase solid solutions throughout the temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In HEA nanoparticles crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution, the combined effect of high configurational entropy together with severe lattice distortion suppresses atomic diffusion and phase separation at elevated temperatures. This interplay governs whether the nanoparticles maintain structural and chemical stability across the catalytic and thermoelectric operating range of 473–1923 K.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equiatomic ratios forming a single-phase solid solution (e.g., FCC or BCC structure) with a uniform elemental distribution.
drafts.intervention: Subject the nanoparticles to thermal cycling and steady-state operation in the range 473–1923 K under catalytic/thermoelectric conditions.
drafts.conditions: Under inert or controlled (reducing) atmospheres in operando catalytic or thermoelectric devices where the temperature is ramped and maintained within the specified range.
drafts.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion induced by atomic size mismatches, which in concert with high mixing entropy, produces high diffusion barriers.
drafts.mechanism: High configurational entropy lowers the free energy of the disordered, single-phase state, while the lattice distortion resulting from moderate differences in atomic radii creates kinetic barriers that suppress atomic diffusion and phase segregation, thereby maintaining both structural and chemical stability despite high temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with relatively low atomic size dispersion (e.g., <15% difference) will retain their single-phase solid solution structure and homogeneous elemental distribution during high-temperature operation. In contrast, nanoparticles with larger size mismatches are predicted to show evidence of phase separation or chemical ordering at high temperatures, leading to degraded catalytic/thermoelectric performance.
drafts.baseline: The uniformly mixed, single-phase solid solution structure of the as-synthesized HEA nanoparticles at room temperature.
drafts.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold provided that the constituent elements have atomic size differences within moderate limits (approximately under 15%) and that the nanoparticles are tested under atmospheres that do not excessively oxidize or otherwise chemically alter the surface beyond thermal effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of HEA nanoparticles that are identical in elemental count but systematically vary the degree of atomic size mismatch (e.g., by choosing metal sets with smaller versus larger atomic radii differences). Subject these samples to identical thermal cycling and continuous operation within 473–1923 K under catalytic/thermoelectric conditions while monitoring for phase changes and elemental segregation using in situ characterization techniques.
measurements: In situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor phase evolution and detect any new phase formation
High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess atomic-scale elemental distribution
Performance metrics from catalytic or thermoelectric tests to correlate structural changes with functional degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with low atomic size mismatch (predicted to be stabilized by high entropy and lattice distortion) exhibit phase separation or significant chemical segregation comparable to those with high mismatches under identical thermal conditions, then the hypothesis—that the interplay between configurational entropy and lattice distortion governs stability—is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In equimolar HEA nanoparticles, the high configurational entropy together with lattice distortion creates large energetic barriers that prevent atomic diffusion and phase segregation, thereby preserving the uniform solid solution structure (both chemically and crystallographically) over the full catalytic and thermoelectric temperature range (473–1923 K).
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a single-phase random solid solution with minimal initial short-range chemical ordering.
drafts.intervention: Expose the HEA nanoparticles to a controlled high-temperature environment spanning 473–1923 K under inert (non-oxidative) conditions representative of catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges.
drafts.conditions: Heating under inert atmosphere with controlled temperature ramp rates and fixed dwell times at target temperatures; no reactive atmosphere present to confound the intrinsic thermodynamic stability.
drafts.structural_mediator: High configurational entropy and the resulting lattice distortion.
drafts.mechanism: The high mixing entropy stabilizes the random elemental arrangement by lowering the overall free energy, while severe lattice distortion introduces kinetic barriers that slow atomic diffusion. This combined effect prevents phase separation or ordering transitions even under extreme thermal conditions, maintaining structural and chemical uniformity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The equimolar HEA nanoparticles will retain their single-phase solid-solution structure with only minor, non-disruptive local short-range ordering, as evidenced by stable X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns and uniform chemical mapping (e.g., TEM/EDX) throughout the 473–1923 K range.
drafts.baseline: The initial room temperature state showing a homogeneous, disordered solid solution phase.
drafts.boundary: A controlled comparison with nanoparticles of a similar overall composition but with fewer alloying elements (e.g., a ternary or quaternary alloy) that exhibit a lower configurational entropy, which are expected to show phase segregation or ordering transitions upon heating.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: (i) equimolar HEA nanoparticles (5+ metals) synthesized in a homogenous solid solution; and (ii) control nanoparticles with similar average metal content but with fewer components (lower configurational entropy). Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling between 473 K and 1923 K under an inert atmosphere. Utilize in situ high-temperature XRD and electron microscopy (e.g., TEM combined with EDX mapping) to monitor any changes in phase structure and elemental distribution in real time.
measurements: X-ray diffraction to detect any phase transitions or formation of secondary phases
TEM/EDX for chemical mapping to identify any onset of elemental segregation
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to observe enthalpic events associated with ordering or phase separation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the equimolar HEA nanoparticles display clear evidence of phase segregation, formation of ordered or intermetallic phases, or significant changes in lattice structure (as opposed to only minor short-range fluctuations) during or after thermal cycling across the specified temperature range, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy and lattice distortion alone govern the stability would be falsified.
